design_detail: Controlled longitudinal study on a closed residential research unit (NIDA Addiction Research Center, Baltimore, 1987-88): 12 men with severe DSM-III-R cocaine dependence, admitted within 48 hours of last use, and 10 men without substance use disorder (except nicotine), each living on the unit for 28 days; self-rated mood, craving (cocaine group only) and sleep, vital signs and weight on 11 study days, analysed with mixed-design ANOVA (group, time, interaction).
can_establish: The course of self-rated mood, craving and sleep over the first 4 weeks of supervised abstinence in a setting without cocaine or cues, compared with men without drug dependence living on the same unit.
cannot_establish: The course outside a controlled setting (no cocaine, no reminders), in women, in people who binge or smoke crack (10 of 12 injected daily), during the first hours after last use (first measure on admission day, up to 48 hours after use), within the day (one morning measure every 2 to 4 days), or of sleep measured objectively.

sample.recruitment: Consecutively self-referred men recruited through newspaper and radio advertisements and notices to treatment clinics and emergency departments in Baltimore: 30 people with cocaine dependence made appointments, 16 came, 14 were admitted and 12 completed; 18 controls made appointments and 10 were admitted and completed (p. 862). Participants were paid on completion ($16.50 a day; $50 for those who left early).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cocaine group: severe active DSM-III-R cocaine dependence; one gram or more a week for at least 12 weeks; a positive urine test for cocaine; willing to stay on a closed unit for 4 to 6 weeks. Excluded: other current substance abuse or dependence except nicotine; positive urine for drugs other than THC and cocaine; medical illness; psychosis or cognitive incapacity; infectious disease; illiteracy; treatment required by courts or employers. Controls: the same, with no lifetime substance use disorder except nicotine (p. 862).
sample.demographics: Cocaine group against controls: mean age 28.1 (SEM 1.9) against 32.1 (1.3); 92% against 80% Black; education 11.5 against 11.2 years; employed 50% against 30%; antisocial personality disorder 58% against 0%; current nicotine dependence 83% against 30% (Table 1, p. 863).
sample.attrition: Two of 14 men in the cocaine group left (on days 3 and 5) and were excluded; all 10 controls completed (p. 862).
sample.selection_effects: Self-referred, paid men willing to live on a locked unit for a month; completers only; 10 of the 12 injected daily rather than binging or smoking (p. 867).

exposure.measurement: Cocaine dependence diagnosed by one psychiatrist with the SADS-L supplemented by questionnaires; recent use confirmed by urine benzoylecgonine on admission and, in 8 men, by sputum and urine over the first 12 hours, consistent with last use no earlier than 48 hours before admission (p. 864).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions (self-report, Table 1, p. 863): 6.7 g a week (SEM 0.4) in the 4 weeks before evaluation and 5.3 g (0.3) in the week before admission; use on 10.8 of the previous 14 days; dependence for 3.7 years; intravenous 10, smoked 1, intranasal 1.
exposure.polysubstance: Cannabis was allowed: 4 of 12 in the cocaine group and 2 of 10 controls had THC-positive urine on day 1; 42% of the cocaine group had past cannabis dependence; cigarettes were allowed on the unit (pp. 863-864).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Daily observed urine tests showed no drug use on the unit (p. 864); last use within 48 hours before day 1.

comparison.controls: Ten men without lifetime substance use disorder (except nicotine), living on the same unit under the same procedures.
comparison.matching: Not matched; no significant differences in age, race, education, employment, marital status or other axis I disorders, but antisocial personality disorder and nicotine dependence were more common in the cocaine group (Table 1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Mood before cocaine use unknown; SCL-90-R scores for the week before intake were higher in the cocaine group on every factor (Table 1).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Thirty per cent of controls had current nicotine dependence; none had another substance use disorder.

outcomes.instruments: Profile of Mood States (65 adjectives), Beck Depression Inventory (13-item), a 100-point visual analogue scale of craving over the past 24 hours (cocaine group only; controls could not rate it), the St Mary's Sleep Questionnaire, resting heart rate, blood pressure and weight, on days 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 14, 18, 21, 25 and 28, between 9 AM and noon (p. 863).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard instruments; the authors note that self-reported sleep can differ from sleep measured by EEG (p. 867).
outcomes.operationalization: Change over time and differences between groups; phases judged from the shape of the curves, without a statistical test.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Self-report; participants and staff knew who was in which group.

analysis.effect_sizes: F ratios only (Table 2; df 1,20 for group, 10,200 for time and interaction, 10,110 for craving): Beck depression 13.949, 10.670, 8.526 (all P<.01); total mood distress 5.082 (P<.05), 9.359, 5.537 (P<.01); depression/dejection 8.806, 5.586, 3.744 (P<.01); tension/anxiety 5.681 (P<.05), 6.483, 5.431 (P<.01); vigor not significant; craving time 17.270 (P<.01). Sleep: difficulty falling asleep, group 10.428 (P<.01) with no time effect; clear-headed on arising, interaction 2.001 (P<.05); the other sleep factors showed time effects only. Heart rate group 4.360 and interaction 1.979 (P<.05); weight group 6.806 (P<.05) and time 31.838 (P<.01). Weight gain 4.6 kg (6.5%) against 3.8 kg (4.3%); heart rate up 10.9 beats a minute against down 2.3 from day 1 to day 28. Daily means appear only in Figures 1 to 4 (values not extracted).
analysis.selective_reporting: All measures are tabulated in Table 2; physiological results are reported elsewhere.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the cocaine group, self-rated mood distress, depression and craving were highest on admission day and lower over the 28 days, mostly within about 2 weeks, with significant group, time and interaction effects; reports of sleep did not differ from controls except more difficulty falling asleep; both groups' sleep improved over time.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says mood distress and craving “decreased gradually and steadily”, and the Comment that the changes were not cyclical or phasic and that short-term abstinence describes them better than withdrawal (pp. 861, 866-867). Gaps: (1) no test of a phasic or non-steady pattern was done, and the plotted means of several mood scales rise again around days 7 to 9 before falling (editors' reading of Figure 1; no values extracted); (2) the setting had no cocaine and no reminders of it, which the authors name as a possible reason for the difference from outpatient reports; (3) the first measure came up to 48 hours after last use, so the earliest part of a crash may have been missed.

timeline.event: Gawin & Kleber, clinical case series proposing crash, withdrawal and extinction phases.
Brower & Paredes letter and the reply by Kleber & Gawin on whether crash and withdrawal are distinct (as described, p. 861).
This controlled residential study: steady improvement without phases.

replication.where_it_stands: The first controlled residential test of the phase model read here; it found steady improvement without phases in a setting free of cocaine and cues. A sleep-laboratory study of inpatient abstinence already in the library (Morgan et al., 2010) adds that measured sleep worsened while self-rated sleep improved.

funding.funder: Not stated; the study was done at the NIDA Addiction Research Center by NIDA staff (affiliations, p. 861).
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed; the opinions are stated to be the authors' own, not NIDA's (p. 861).
funding.affiliations_note: NIDA, Rockville, and the Addiction Research Center, Baltimore; the first author was the psychiatrist and case manager who saw all participants 5 days a week.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people stopping cocaine after binge use, in residential and community settings, with momentary ratings of mood and craving several times a day from the last dose for 10 weeks, actigraphy, and a pre-specified test for phases.

domains.note: The groups differed in antisocial personality disorder (58% against 0%), nicotine and past cannabis dependence, and in time with staff (more counselling for the cocaine group); 3 of 12 in the cocaine group and 7 of 10 controls had pituitary challenge tests (levodopa, protirelin); none adjusted for.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Dependence diagnosed by one psychiatrist; time, amount and purity of the last dose not standardized (p. 867).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Paid, self-referred men willing to live on a locked unit; 16 of 30 came to evaluation and only completers were analysed, which can favour people whose distress eased.
Counselling, daily psychiatrist contact, recreation and the challenge tests could change mood; acetaminophen in two men of each group.
Two of 14 in the cocaine group left early and were excluded; craving not rated by controls.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Unblinded self-ratings once every 2 to 4 days in the morning; no objective sleep measure.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: All 21 measures are reported in Table 2.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E for a non-randomized two-group comparison. The time course within the cocaine group is the main finding; it is vulnerable to selection (completers in a locked unit) and to the setting, and the comparison with controls is confounded by personality disorder and attention. It is cited for the course of self-rated symptoms in a cue-free residential setting, not for people stopping at home.

key_findings.finding: Twelve men with severe cocaine dependence (10 injecting daily) and 10 men without drug dependence lived on a closed research unit for 28 days; 30 men with cocaine dependence had made appointments, 16 came, 14 were admitted and 2 left on days 3 and 5.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Subjects and Methods › Subjects, 8th and 9th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Measures (Profile of Mood States, Beck Depression Inventory, craving scale for the past 24 hours, St Mary's Sleep Questionnaire, vital signs, weight) on days 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 14, 18, 21, 25 and 28 between 9 AM and noon; controls did not rate craving.
All men in the cocaine group had used cocaine within 48 hours before admission (urine and sputum findings consistent); daily urine tests showed no drug use on the unit.

Mood distress and depression scores were raised in the cocaine group and changed over time differently from controls: Beck depression F = 13.949 (group), 10.670 (time), 8.526 (interaction); total mood distress 5.082, 9.359, 5.537; vigor did not differ.
Craving was highest on the day of admission and fell significantly over the 28 days (F = 17.270, df 10,110, P<.01).
key_findings.locator: Outcome › Craving for Cocaine (p. 864); Figure 2 and Table 2 (p. 865)

key_findings.finding: Sleep: no group differences except more difficulty falling asleep in the cocaine group throughout (group F = 10.428) and more improvement in clear-headedness on waking (interaction F = 2.001); all sleep measures except difficulty falling asleep improved in both groups.
key_findings.locator: Outcome › Self-reports of Sleep (p. 864); Figure 3 and Table 2 (p. 865)

key_findings.finding: Weight gain did not differ (4.6 kg or 6.5% against 3.8 kg or 4.3%); heart rate rose 10.9 beats a minute in the cocaine group and fell 2.3 in controls from day 1 to day 28; blood pressure did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Outcome › Weight, Heart Rate, and Blood Pressure (p. 864, continued p. 866)

key_findings.finding: The authors report that mood, craving and night waking improved gradually and were not cyclical or phasic during the first 4 weeks, unlike the earlier phase models, and suggest the cue-free controlled setting as a reason; they were surprised that both groups' sleep improved, possibly from adapting to the unit.

In Figure 1, the cocaine group's mean scores on several Profile of Mood States scales (tension, depression, anger, fatigue, confusion, total distress) fall from day 1 to day 5, rise again around days 7 to 9, then fall and stay low from about day 11 or 14; the Beck depression line falls more evenly.
key_findings.note: Editors' description of the plotted means; no values were extracted, and the error bars are wide.

key_findings.finding: Limitations named by the authors: small all-male, mostly Black sample of mostly daily injectors; reliance on self-report; the experimental setting; no standard last dose or uniform starting point; THC-positive participants; no sleep EEG; only the first month; morning measures only.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives height as 2.8 (SEM 0.1) and 2.9 (0.1) metres, which is impossible for adults.
reporting_issues.consequence: A unit or transcription error; heights are not used in any analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives use on 10.8 (SEM 0.02) of the previous 14 days; Table 1 gives 10.8 (0.2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the table value is the plausible one.

reporting_issues.issue: The group effect for anger/hostility is marked P<.05 in Table 2, but F = 4.347 on 1 and 20 degrees of freedom gives p = 0.0501 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Borderline; anger/hostility should not be counted as clearly different between groups.
